heath_proof: For let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the sixth apotome AD; I say that the “side” of the area AB is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. For let DG be the annex to AD; therefore AG, GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, neither of them is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on the whole AG is greater than the square on the annex DG by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG. [X. Deff. III. 6] Since then the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG, therefore, if there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on DG and deficient by a square figure, it will divide it into incommensurable parts. [X. 18] Let then DG be bisected at E, let there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure, and let it be the rectangle AF, FG; therefore AF is incommensurable in length with FG. But, as AF is to FG, so is AI to FK. [VI. 1] therefore AI is incommensurable with FK. [X. 11] And, since AG, AC are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, AK is medial. [X. 21] Again, since AC, DG are rational straight lines and incommensurable in length, DK is also medial. [X. 21] Now, since AG, GD are commensurable in square only, therefore AG is incommensurable in length with GD. But, as AG is to GD, so is AK to KD; [VI. 1] therefore AK is incommensurable with KD. [X. 11] Now let the square LM be constructed equal to AI, and let NO equal to FK, and about the same angle, be subtracted; therefore the squares LM, NO are about the same diameter. [VI. 26] Let PR be their diameter, and let the figure be drawn. Then in manner similar to the above we can prove that LN is the “side” of the area AB. I say that LN is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. For, since AK was proved medial and is equal to the squares on LP, PN, therefore the sum of the squares on LP, PN is medial. Again, since DK was proved medial and is equal to twice the rectangle LP, PN, twice the rectangle LP, PN is also medial. And, since AK was proved incommensurable with DK, the squares on LP, PN are also incommensurable with twice the rectangle LP, PN. And, since AI is incommensurable with FK, therefore the square on LP is also incommensurable with the square on PN; therefore LP, PN are straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, twice the rectangle contained by them medial, and further the squares on them incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them. Therefore LN is the irrational straight line called that which produces with a medial area a medial whole; [X. 78] and it is the “side” of the area AB. Therefore the “side” of the area is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.

10.96
**Statement:** If an area be contained by a rational straight line and a sixth apotome, the âsideâ of the area is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.

**Step 1.** Let the area AB be contained by the rational straight line AC and the sixth apotome AD. I say that the "side" of the area AB is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole.

**Step 2.** Since AD is a sixth apotome, let DG be the annex to AD, so that AG is the whole and GD is the annex. By the definition of a sixth apotome (D10.3.6), AG and GD are rational straight lines commensurable in square only, neither AG nor GD is commensurable in length with the rational straight line AC set out, and the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable in length with AG.

**Step 3.** Since the square on AG is greater than the square on GD by the square on a straight line incommensurable with AG, if there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the fourth part of the square on GD and deficient by a square figure, it will divide AG into parts which are incommensurable in length [10.18].

**Step 4.** Let DG be bisected at the point E, let there be applied to AG a parallelogram equal to the square on EG and deficient by a square figure, and let it be the rectangle AF by FG. Then AF is incommensurable in length with FG [10.18].

**Step 5.** Now since AG is incommensurable in length with AC, both AG and GD being incommensurable in length with AC, and since AG and GD are rational, the rectangle contained by AC and AG is medial, and likewise the rectangle contained by AC and DG is medial [10.21].

**Step 6.** Apply to AC the rectangle AH equal to the square on AG, producing AH as breadth, and apply to AC the rectangle GK equal to the square on GD, producing GK as breadth. Then since the square on AG is incommensurable with the square on GD (for AG and GD are commensurable in square only, hence their squares are commensurable, but AG is incommensurable in length with GD, and since each is rational, the rectangle AG by GD is irrational; however, we note that since AG and GD are rational and commensurable in square only, the squares on AG and on GD are each rational areas), and these squares are applied to the rational line AC, the breadths AH and GK are each rational and incommensurable in length with AC [10.22].

**Step 7.** Since AF is incommensurable in length with FG, the square on AF is incommensurable with the rectangle AF by FG [10.11]. But the square on AG is commensurable with the square on AF, since AG is commensurable in square with AF (they are both derived from the same partition); and the rectangle AG by GD is commensurable with the rectangle AF by FG, since AG by GD equals twice AF by FG by the properties of the bisection and the application [2.5]. Therefore the square on AG is incommensurable with the rectangle AG by GD [10.13].

**Step 8.** But the square on AG equals AH (as applied to AC), and the rectangle AG by GD, taken twice, equals the area by which AH exceeds GK applied to AC. Thus AH is incommensurable with the rectangle contained by AG and GD applied to AC. Hence the breadth corresponding to AH is incommensurable in length with the breadth corresponding to twice the rectangle AG by GD, both being applied to the rational line AC [10.11].

**Step 9.** Now since the rectangle AC by AG is medial [Step 5], the area AH (the square on AG applied to AC) has AH as breadth, and this area is rational (square on a rational line), making the breadth rational but incommensurable in length with AC [10.22]. Similarly for GK.

**Step 10.** Since AG by GD equals the rectangle contained by AG and GD, and twice this rectangle applied to AC gives the difference of areas corresponding to the decomposition, and since AG and GD are commensurable in square only with neither commensurable in length with AC, twice the rectangle AG by GD is medial [10.21], applied to the rational line AC, gives a breadth which is rational and incommensurable in length with AC.

**Step 11.** Moreover, AH is incommensurable with GK applied in this way [from Step 8], so the breadths are incommensurable in length, and AH and GK are both medial areas. Further, since AF is incommensurable in length with FG, and the areas corresponding to the squares on AF and on FG (applied to AC) produce the sum of squares which is medial, and twice the rectangle AF by FG applied to AC is also medial, and these two are incommensurable with each other [from Steps 7-8].

**Step 12.** Let the square on MN equal the rectangle AC by AF (i.e., the area corresponding to AF), and let the square on NO equal the rectangle AC by FG, with MN and NO laid along the same straight line. Then the rectangle MN by NO is equal to half of the rectangle AC by AG times the appropriate factor, and in particular MO is a straight line such that MN and NO are incommensurable in square [10.11, from AF incommensurable with FG applied through 10.22].

**Step 13.** The sum of the squares on MN and on NO equals the rectangle AC by AG (since AF + FG = AG, the rectangles AC by AF and AC by FG sum to AC by AG), which is a medial area [Step 5, since AG is incommensurable in length with AC and both are rational, giving a medial rectangle by 10.21].

**Step 14.** Twice the rectangle MN by NO equals the rectangle AC by DG. This is because AG by GD = 2(AF by FG) from the bisection at E and the application [2.5], and the rectangle AC by GD = AC times GD, which relates to twice the rectangle of the parts. Since GD is incommensurable in length with AC and both are rational, AC by GD is medial [10.21].

**Step 15.** Since the square on AG is incommensurable with the rectangle AG by GD [Step 7], and the square on AG corresponds to the sum of squares on MN and NO (as AC by AG), while the rectangle AG by GD corresponds to twice the rectangle MN by NO (as AC by GD), the sum of the squares on MN and NO is incommensurable with twice the rectangle MN by NO.

**Step 16.** Therefore MN and NO are two straight lines incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on them is medial [Step 13], twice the rectangle contained by them is medial [Step 14], and the sum of the squares on them is incommensurable with twice the rectangle contained by them [Step 15].

**Step 17.** Therefore MO = MN + NO is the side of the sum of two medial areas [10.41]. Now MN - NO (or NO subtracted from MN, taking whichever is greater) gives a straight line whose square equals the area AB. More precisely, the square on the whole line MO corresponds to AC by AD plus 2(rect MN by NO), while we need the "side" of the area AC by AD. Since AD = AG - GD, the rectangle AC by AD = AC by AG - AC by GD = (sq on MN + sq on NO) - 2(rect MN by NO) = sq on (MN - NO), taking the appropriate difference.

**Step 18.** Therefore the "side" of the area AB is MN - NO (the remainder when the lesser is subtracted from the greater). Since MN and NO are incommensurable in square, the sum of the squares on them is medial, twice the rectangle contained by them is medial, and the squares on them are incommensurable with twice the rectangle, MN - NO is the straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole [10.78].

**Step 19.** Therefore, if an area be contained by a rational straight line and a sixth apotome, the "side" of the area is a straight line which produces with a medial area a medial whole. Q.E.D.
